Title: Enhancing wind power forecasting accuracy through LSTM with adaptive wind speed calibration (C-LSTM)
Text:
Enhancing wind power forecasting 
accuracy through LSTM with 
adaptive wind speed calibration 
(C-LSTM)
Ding Wang1, Min Xu2, Zhu Guangming1, Futao Luo5, Jiaxin Gao3,4 & Yuntian Chen4,6
Wind power constitutes a pivotal component in the quest for carbon neutrality, serving as a principal 
renewable energy source. Enhancing the accuracy of wind power forecasting facilitates more efficient 
exploitation of this resource, with deep-learning models, notably Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), 
proving effective in advancing forecasting capabilities within this domain. Nevertheless, the accuracy 
of wind power forecasting is undermined by the inaccurate forecasted wind speed, which diminish the 
reliability of such predictions. To address this challenge, we propose the model “LSTM with Adaptive 
Wind Speed Calibration (C-LSTM)”, which integrates a mechanism into LSTM that autonomously 
calibrates forecasted wind speed during the training and inference phase. Specifically, considering the 
inherent continuity of wind speed, C-LSTM fuses historical wind speed with forecasted wind speed 
using adaptive weighting parameters. This integration is harmonized with the concurrent updating 
of the other parameters of C-LSTM, thereby ensuring a dynamic adaptation process that bolsters the 
model’s capacity to coordinate discrepancies between forecasted and actual wind speeds. Experiments 
conducted across 25 distinct wind turbines have demonstrated that C-LSTM significantly outperforms 
LSTM in both Mean Squared Error (MSE) and accuracy metrics when the latter directly incorporates 
forecasted or historical wind speeds. This disparity underscores the efficacy of the adaptive wind speed 
calibration technique employed within the C-LSTM framework.
Keywords  Wind power forecasting, LSTM, Adaptive wind speed calibration, C-LSTM

Wind power has emerged as a rapidly expanding global energy source, exerting a profound influence on both 
industrial productivity and daily life1. Wind energy production is notably distinguished by its intermittent and 
fluctuating characteristics, which pose significant challenges for energy management and grid stability. The 
absence of a robust and cost-effective energy storage system mandates the instantaneous utilization of generated 
power immediately after its production. Consequently, accurate wind power forecasting becomes vital for the 
proficient management of wind farms and wind-dependent energy systems, facilitating their optimal integration 
into the energy grid2. Accurate forecasting allows for better scheduling of maintenance, more efficient dispatch 
of conventional power plants, and enhanced overall grid reliability. Nevertheless, the inaccuracy of forecasted 
wind speed3,4, which stands in contrast to the relative stability of solar radiation in photovoltaic energy systems, 
amplifies forecasting errors and considerably heightens the complexity of wind power forecasting tasks. These 
inaccuracies in wind speed forecasts can lead to suboptimal energy dispatch, increased operational costs, and 
potential disruptions to the balance of supply and demand within the grid. Therefore, developing sophisticated 
forecasting models that can mitigate these inaccuracies is critical for maximizing the benefits of wind energy and 
ensuring its seamless integration into the broader energy infrastructure.

Wind power forecasting encompasses a range of time horizons, including both short-term and long-term 
predictions5. Day-ahead forecasting, which pertains to predictions made for the following day, plays a critical 
role in the operational planning and market integration of wind farms. This type of forecasting is particularly 
significant for optimizing the utilization of wind power, as it directly impacts decisions related to energy trading 
and scheduling within electricity markets6. Consequently, this study places a particular emphasis on day-
ahead forecasting of wind power. Scholarly interest in wind power forecasting has surged, culminating in the 
development of a diverse array of forecasting models. These models can largely be categorized into two primary 
groups: those grounded in domain knowledge (knowledge-based) and those rooted in historical data (data-
driven).
Knowledge-based models harness physical principles to simulate and forecast wind power, leveraging deep 
insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing wind dynamics. Notable examples include innovative 
smoothing methodologies addressing physical problems associated with wind power7, such as turbulence and 
gustiness, which can significantly impact the performance and reliability of wind turbines. Another example is the 
use of wavelet decomposition coupled with AdaBoost techniques for forecasting8, which decomposes the wind 
speed signal into different frequency components and applies ensemble learning to improve prediction accuracy. 
Moreover, sophisticated Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) frameworks integrating climatic simulations 
and wind power curve analyses to provide detailed forecasts9,10. These frameworks utilize meteorological data 
to predict future wind conditions, which are then translated into expected power outputs using turbine-specific 
wind power curves11,12. These knowledge-based models provide interpretative clarity and a strong theoretical 
foundation, but they require extensive physical feature extraction and may not fully leverage the richness of 
historical wind power data.
Conversely, data-driven models leverage historical datasets for forecasting purposes, divided into classical 
statistical methodologies and deep-learning-based models13. Traditional statistical applications, such as 
autoregressive moving average (ARMA)14 and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA)15, excel in 
short-term predictions due to their ability to model linear dependencies in time series data. However, these 
models falter when the forecast horizon extends, as they struggle to capture the complex and nonlinear dynamics 
that are inherent in long-term wind power forecasting. The advent of deep-learning has introduced a suite of 
advanced models that are capable of capturing intricate nonlinear relationships and have shown significant 
promise in handling complex time-series data. Examples include the multilayer perceptron (MLP)16,17, which 
is a feedforward neural network architecture that can learn complex mappings between inputs and outputs. 
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)18–20 are specifically designed to handle sequential data by maintaining an 
internal state that allows the model to consider past information in its predictions. Variants of RNNs, such 
as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), have been particularly 
successful in wind power forecasting due to their ability to manage long-term dependencies effectively. 
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)21,22, traditionally used in image processing, have also found applications 
in wind power forecasting, particularly when dealing with spatial–temporal data such as wind maps. CNNs 
can extract hierarchical features from multidimensional data, making them useful for scenarios where spatial 
correlations play a significant role. Furthermore, Autoencoders (AEs)23–25 are another class of deep-learning 
models that are adept at unsupervised learning tasks, such as dimensionality reduction and feature learning. 
They can be used to preprocess the input data, extracting meaningful representations that can then be fed into 
other predictive models. Some advanced Transformer-based models26,27 also show significant potential in wind 
power forecasting. These pure data-driven deep-learning models are capable of capturing intricate nonlinear 
relationships and have shown promise in handling complex time-series data. However, they require substantial 
amounts of data to yield satisfactory results and face the challenge of potentially converging to a local minimum 
during training, which can hinder the attainment of optimal prediction accuracy. The incorporation of domain 
knowledge may effectively alleviate these challenges.
Neither knowledge-based models nor data-driven models, when used in isolation, fully address the problem 
of inaccurate forecasted wind speed. It is recognized that combining these two paradigms can lead to more robust 
solutions. Indeed, knowledge and data dual-driven models has been widely utilized in multiple domains28–32. 
In this research, we adopt this hybrid approach to address the issue of inaccuracies in forecasted wind speed 
and to enhance the accuracy of wind power forecasting. Specifically, based on domain knowledge, it is well-
acknowledged that wind speed exhibits a degree of temporal continuity33,34, with the wind speed on any given 
day typically exhibiting correlation with that of the preceding day, barring instances of extreme weather events. 
However, due to the complexity inherent in modeling the precise relationship between wind speeds across 
consecutive days, current forecasted wind speed often fails to adequately incorporate the actual wind speed 
measurements from the previous day4. This oversight in leveraging temporal continuity contributes to a shortfall 
in the accuracy of forecasted wind speed.
In this study, we introduce C-LSTM, an innovative approach that incorporates an adaptive mechanism 
within the LSTM35 architecture for calibrating forecasted wind speeds. Unlike traditional methodologies, our 
model enhances the input to the LSTM by simultaneously incorporating both the actual wind speed from the 
preceding day and the raw forecasted wind speed for the current day. These two inputs are integrated through 
learnable parameters, which are updated alongside the other parameters of the C-LSTM network during 
the training process. This integration allows the model to dynamically adjust its forecasts based on the latest 
available data, resulting in a calibrated and more accurate forecast of wind speed36. This calibrated forecasted 
wind speed, along with historical wind speeds, historical wind power, and other pertinent variables, collectively 
serve as the foundation for the LSTM’s modeling process. By leveraging this enhanced input, C-LSTM aims to 
surmount the challenges posed by the inaccuracy of wind speed forecasts, thereby yielding more precise wind 
power predictions. The superior performance of C-LSTM has been validated across a diverse set of 25 individual 
wind turbines, demonstrating its effectiveness in varied conditions and environments. This extensive validation

In summary, our main contributions of this study include:
•	 This study introduces a novel deep-learning model C-LSTM, which embeds an adaptive mechanism to cali­
brate forecasted wind speeds during both training and inference phases. This innovation addresses a crucial 
limitation in existing wind power forecasting models by enhancing the accuracy of forecasted wind speeds.
•	 Through extensive experiments on 25 different wind turbines, we validate the superior performance of 
C-LSTM. The model consistently achieves lower MSE and higher accuracy in comparison to conventional 
LSTM when confronted with both raw forecasted and historical wind speed data.
Methodology
In this study, we utilize the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model with adaptive wind speed calibration 
(C-LSTM) to forecast wind power and address the challenge of inaccuracy in raw forecasted wind speeds. This 
section begins with an exposition of the fundamental deep-learning model, LSTM, which serves as the backbone 
of the C-LSTM architecture. We then proceed to elucidate the methodology for calibrating forecasted wind 
speeds and detail how this calibrated data is integrated within the C-LSTM framework.
LSTM
Long short-term memory (LSTM) network35, a classic variant in the realm of neural networks, excels in handling 
sequential data. It finds applications across various domains, including weather patterns37, audio signals38 and 
oil well data39.
LSTM is a type of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). RNNs are a class of neural networks designed to 
recognize patterns in sequences of data, such as time series or natural language. Unlike standard feedforward 
neural networks such as MLPs, which assume that inputs are independent of each other, RNNs maintain an 
internal state (hidden state) that allows them to capture information about the past, making them particularly 
well-suited for tasks involving sequential data. The architecture of an RNN includes loops in the network’s 
connections, which enable information to persist. During the forward pass, the network takes both the current 
input and the previous hidden state as inputs to compute the current hidden state and the output. This recurrent 
connection allows the network to have a form of memory, enabling it to use learned information from prior 
inputs to influence the processing of subsequent inputs.
However, traditional RNNs often struggle to maintain information over long periods due to the issues of 
vanishing and exploding gradients. The vanishing gradient problem occurs when the gradients of the error 
function, which are propagated backward through time during training, become very small, leading to minimal 
changes in the weights of early layers. Conversely, the exploding gradient problem happens when these gradients 
become excessively large, potentially causing weights to update unpredictably or diverge.
LSTMs address these issues by introducing a more sophisticated internal structure, as illustrated in Fig. 1. 
Central to this architecture is the cell state Ct, which traverses the LSTM cells, preserving historical information. 
The LSTM cell also comprises a forget gate ft, an input gate it and an output gate ot, collaborating alongside the 
prior hidden state ht-1 and the current input Xt to modulate information retention and introduction. Specifically:
The forget gate, represented by Eq. (1), decides what information to discard from the cell state based on the 
current input and the previous hidden state. The output ft ranges between 0 and 1, which will be multiplied with 
the cell state from previous step in Eq. (4).

Despite its complexity, the design of LSTM effectively mitigates gradient issues, enabling it to perform short-term 
feature extraction similar to that of RNNs while also capturing long-term dependencies29. This dual capability 
renders LSTM highly suitable for wind power forecasting tasks, where the ability to accurately predict power 
generation relies on both recent trends and historical patterns. The ability of LSTM to handle such complex 
sequences makes it an efficient tool for enhancing the precision of wind power predictions, thereby supporting 
more efficient grid management and renewable energy integration.
Adaptive wind speed calibration in C-LSTM
In the proposed C-LSTM model, we enhance the standard LSTM architecture by integrating an adaptive 
calibration mechanism specifically tailored for forecasted wind speeds. Recognizing the inherent continuity 
and temporal correlations present in wind speed data, our approach aims to address the common issue where 
conventional forecasting models may overlook these characteristics. By incorporating historical wind speed 
data, the adaptive calibration mechanism refines the raw forecasted wind speeds, ensuring that the predictions 
are more aligned with real-world patterns. This process is illustrated in Fig. 2, demonstrating how the model 
leverages historical wind speed data to calibrate the forecasted wind speed.
In the figure, different colors and symbols represent specific aspects of the wind power calibration process: 
green denotes the raw forecasted wind speed for the current day, gray represents historical wind speed data from 
the last three days, and blue indicates the historical wind power data from the same period. The symbols tpre, 
t-3, t-2, t-1, and t correspond to the respective time steps, while w signifies the weight factor applied to the raw 
forecasted wind speed. The orange arrow indicates the direction of the calibration process, underscoring the 
significance of historical wind speed data in refining the raw forecasted wind speed to ensure it more accurately 
reflects real-world conditions, thereby enhancing the overall accuracy of wind power forecasts. The blue arrow 
represents the direction of the final wind power forecasting, illustrating the effective utilization of the calibrated 
forecasted wind speed in generating more precise predictions.
The calibration process is mathematically expressed by Eq. (6):

Stc = WStpred + (1 −W) St−1 + b, 
(6)
where Stc represents the calibrated forecasted wind speed for the current day, St−1 signifies the actual wind 
speed from the previous day, and Stpred denotes the raw forecasted wind speed for the current day. W represents 
the adaptive weighting parameters, and b is the intercept term. Both W and b are 144-dimensional vectors, 
aligning with the length of a day’s wind speed. These parameters are integrated into the LSTM architecture 
and are iteratively updated during the training phase alongside other model parameters to optimize the overall 
forecasting accuracy. This adaptive mechanism ensures that the model can dynamically adjust its predictions 
based on historical data, thereby enhancing the reliability and precision of the wind speed forecasts. During the 
testing phase, the parameters W and b are fixed at their optimized values obtained during the training phase, 
ensuring that the calibrated forecast Stc is generated consistently and reliably across new, unseen data.
The inputs to the C-LSTM model are structured in a three-dimensional format: (i) the batch size, which is 
set at 300 for each training iteration; (ii) the time steps, which utilize 576 steps (corresponding to 4 days of 
data sampled at 10-min intervals); and (iii) the feature dimensions, which encompass four distinct features—
historical wind power, historical wind speed, forecasted wind speed, and turbine pitch angle.
The C-LSTM model comprises two LSTM layers, each configured with a hidden layer size of 20. To augment 
the model’s expressive capacity, two fully connected layers are incorporated, facilitating a richer representation 
of the input data and contributing to improved forecasting accuracy. This design ensures that the C-LSTM model 
can effectively capture both temporal dependencies and complex relationships among the input features, thereby 
enhancing its predictive performance.
Experiment
Data description
In this study, we conducted a case study utilizing wind turbine data from Jiangsu Province, China. The dataset 
encompasses comprehensive records from the year 2020 for 25 distinct wind turbines, each featuring four 
key features: pitch angle, historical wind speed, raw forecasted wind speed, and wind power. The relative 
geographical distribution of these wind turbines is provided in Appendix A. The pitch angle controls the blade 
angle to optimize energy capture, ensuring that the turbine blades are positioned to harness the maximum 
amount of wind energy efficiently. Wind speed is a primary driver of turbine operation, directly influencing the 
rotational speed and, consequently, the power output. Wind power output is the electrical energy generated by 
the turbines, which is a critical metric for assessing the performance and efficiency of the wind farms. These 
variables are sampled at a frequency of every 10 min, resulting in approximately 50,000 data points per turbine 
over the course of the year. This high-resolution dataset provides a detailed view of wind dynamics and power 
generation patterns.
A visual representation of the feature distributions across these turbines, depicted in Fig. 3, reveals notable 
similarities among their statistical distributions. These similarities suggest a consistent pattern in the behavior 
of the turbines, which can be attributed to the shared environmental conditions and operational settings within 
the same geographical region. This consistency is crucial for developing and validating forecasting models, as 
it allows for the identification of common trends and the establishment of a reliable baseline for comparative 
analysis of wind power forecasting.
Data from January to October is used for training, while data from November and December is reserved for 
testing. The input data spans a duration of four days, encapsulating the features of the pitch angle, historical wind 
speed, forecasted wind speed, and historical wind power for each turbine. Figure 4 illustrates the comparison 
between actual and raw forecasted wind speeds over a given period. Specifically, the forecasted wind speeds 
represent predictions made 24 h in advance. While the overall trend in forecasted wind speeds closely resembles 
that of the actual wind speeds, discrepancies, particularly in finer details, are notably evident. These discrepancies 
highlight the challenges in accurately capturing the rapid fluctuations and local variations in wind conditions, 
which are critical for precise wind power forecasting.
Moreover, Fig. 5 shows wind power curves11,40 derived from actual and forecasted wind speeds, highlighting 
the differences between them. The wind power curve is a graphical representation that depicts the relationship 
between wind speed and the power output of a wind turbine. Typically, as wind speed increases, so does the 
power output, up to a point where the turbine reaches its rated capacity. In the figure, the curves derived from 
actual wind speeds provide a more accurate and smooth representation of the true wind power relationship, 
reflecting the expected power output under real-world conditions. In contrast, the wind power curves generated 
from raw forecasted wind speeds exhibit more variability and incorporate a higher degree of noise, which reduces 
the precision of the power output estimates. This increased noise and variability can be attributed to inaccuracies 
in the wind speed forecasts, which often fail to fully capture the nuanced and dynamic nature of atmospheric 
conditions. Such discrepancies highlight the inaccuracies in raw forecasted wind speed and underscore the 
necessity for calibrating these forecasts.
Experiment setting
In the wind power forecasting experiments, C-LSTM employs a sliding window approach to generate both 
training and testing samples. This process begins with an initial input window that spans the first four days of 
historical wind power, pitch angle, historical wind speed, and forecasted wind speed. Since C-LSTM is a day-
ahead forecasting model, the forecasting horizon is the future 24 h (144 time steps). Therefore, the corresponding 
output window includes the wind power data for the subsequent fifth day, forming the first sample. This 
initial window captures a sufficient temporal context to enable the model to learn the underlying patterns and

standardized form, typically with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. This process ensures that the input 
features are on a common scale, which is essential for optimizing the performance of machine learning models, 
particularly those that are sensitive to the scale of the input data, such as LSTMs. By applying standardization,

The training batch size is set to 300, and the training epoch is set to 50, with an early stopping patience of 
5 to prevent overfitting. The widely-used MSE loss function is employed, and optimization is performed using 
the Adam optimizer, which is known for its efficiency and performance in handling sparse gradients and noisy 
data. Each experimental result is averaged from five independent runs to ensure robustness and reliability of the 
outcomes. The experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU with a memory capacity 
of 24 GB, providing the computational capacity necessary for efficient model training and evaluation.

Wind power forecasting results
The test set results of C-LSTM are presented in Table 1. For comparison, several baseline configurations within 
the LSTM framework were evaluated to assess the effectiveness of the C-LSTM approach. Specifically, these 
configurations included using forecasted wind speeds directly (labeled as ‘Forecasted’ in the table), incorporating 
historical wind speeds without modification (referred to as ‘Historical’), and implementing a balanced linear 
combination of forecasted and historical wind speeds (with each contributing 50%, labeled as ‘Combined’) 
as inputs to the LSTM. The table lists the average accuracy, MSE, N_RMSE and N_MAE across all 25 wind 
turbines for each of these configurations. Additionally, the table provides the best and worst accuracy and MSE 
achieved among the turbines, offering a comprehensive overview of the performance across the entire dataset. 
The inclusion of the best and worst accuracy, MSE, N_RMSE and N_MAE scores further aids in understanding 
the variability in performance across the different wind turbines. This information is crucial for identifying any 
outliers or specific conditions under which the models perform exceptionally well or poorly, which could inform 
future improvements and refinements in the C-LSTM model.
Table 1 demonstrates that C-LSTM outperforms the other baseline configurations in both accuracy and MSE 
metrics. Specifically, the incorporation of an adaptive wind speed calibration mechanism within the C-LSTM 
framework improves accuracy by 0.4% and reduces the MSE, N_RMSE and N_MAE by 0.012, 0.013 and 0.010 
compared to using uncalibrated forecasted wind speeds. This enhancement indicates that the dynamic adjustment 
of forecasted wind speeds based on real-time data contributes significantly to the precision of wind power 
predictions. When compared to the use of historical wind speed data alone, C-LSTM further enhances accuracy 
by 0.5% and reduces the MSE, N_RMSE and N_MAE by 0.019, 0.016 and 0.012. This improvement underscores 
the value of combining historical data with adaptive, calibrated forecasts to achieve a more robust predictive 
model. Historical data provides a stable reference point, but it lacks the dynamic adjustment capabilities that 
C-LSTM introduces. Notably, a simplistic linear combination of forecasted and historical wind speeds, with each 
contributing equally (the ‘Combined’ approach), does not effectively calibrate forecasted winds, as evidenced by 
its inferior performance relative to uncalibrated forecasted wind speeds. This finding highlights the limitations of 
fixed-weight averaging strategies and underscores the superiority of C-LSTM’s adaptive calibration mechanism. 
The learnable parameters within C-LSTM allow for a more nuanced and context-aware adjustment of forecasted 
speeds, leading to better overall performance. C-LSTM’s improved accuracy and reduced error rate are essential 
for optimizing wind farm operations, enhancing grid stability, and ensuring that renewable energy sources are 
integrated effectively into the energy system.
Furthermore, the boxplots of accuracy for the different methods across 25 wind turbines are shown in Fig. 6. 
The visual representations clearly demonstrate that C-LSTM not only achieves more accurate predictions but 
also exhibits greater stability in its forecasts. The narrower spread of the C-LSTM boxplot indicates a more 
consistent performance, with fewer outliers and a tighter clustering around the median, suggesting that the 
model’s predictions are consistently reliable. In contrast, the wider spread and presence of outliers in the boxplots 
of the baselines indicate less consistent performance, highlighting the superiority of C-LSTM in both accuracy 
and stability.
For comparative purposes, we also examined scenarios using actual wind speed data (which is unattainable 
in real-time deployment) and scenarios where wind speed data is not utilized, relying solely on historical wind 
power to perform autoregressive forecasting, as depicted in Table 2. The table reveals that utilizing ideal, real-time 
wind speed information enables remarkably precise wind power forecasts, achieving the highest accuracy and 
lowest MSE, N_RMSE and N_MAE among all tested configurations. This ideal scenario, while impractical for 
operational use, sets a benchmark for the maximum achievable forecasting accuracy. Conversely, relying solely 
on historical wind power for autoregressive forecasting leads to a significant decline in the model’s predictive 
performance, with higher MSE, N_RMSE and N_MAE values indicating greater discrepancies between predicted 
and actual wind power. These findings further emphasize the critical role of accurate wind speed in forecasting 
wind power and underscore the necessity of precise wind speed calibration to enhance forecasting performance.

Figure 7 showcases the predictive performance of C-LSTM on a specific wind turbine over a certain period, 
including magnified views of several intervals. For comparison, the figure also displays the results of the baseline 
LSTM using raw forecasted wind speeds. The blue line represents the actual wind power values, the green line 
denotes the predicted values generated by the C-LSTM model, and the red line represents the predictions from 
the baseline LSTM. Evidently, the forecasts produced by C-LSTM more closely mirror the actual wind power 
trends, exhibiting exceptional alignment and capturing subtle deviations in wind power fluctuations. This visual 
representation underscores the model’s capability to provide predictions that are not only directionally accurate 
but also detailed in reflecting the dynamic changes inherent in wind power, thereby validating the effectiveness 
of the adaptive wind speed calibration mechanism employed by C-LSTM. The close match between the actual 
and predicted values demonstrates the model’s robustness and reliability in forecasting, which is essential for 
effective wind farm management and grid integration.
Additionally, an intersection chart based on the ground truth and predictions of C-LSTM is shown in Fig. 8. 
The proximity of the data points in the intersection graph to the 45-degree diagonal indicates the accuracy of 
C-LSTM; the closer they are, the higher the accuracy. As can be observed from the figure, the intersection of the 
true values and the predictions of C-LSTM closely aligns with the 45-degree diagonal, indicating that C-LSTM 
achieves high prediction accuracy.
Furthermore, we have plotted the wind power curve derived from the calibrated wind speed and wind power 
data, as shown in Fig. 9. Although the calibrated wind power curve is not as smooth as the actual wind power 
curve (as seen in the left subplot of Fig. 5), its performance is noticeably better than the wind power curve 
obtained using raw forecasted wind speed (as shown in the right subplot of Fig. 5). This comparison highlights 
the effectiveness of the adaptive calibration mechanism in enhancing the quality of the forecasted wind speed.
The adaptive wind speed calibration is a key differentiator from the standard LSTM, which directly uses raw 
forecasted wind speeds without adjustments, and this calibration mechanism is crucial for achieving better wind 
power forecasting performance. The calibration mechanism is designed to account for the temporal continuity 
and correlations in wind speed data, enabling the model to automatically adjust the influence of the forecasted 
wind speed based on historical wind speed. This reduces the impact of inaccuracies in the raw forecasted wind 
speeds. The effectiveness of this wind speed calibration is demonstrated by the comparison between Fig. 9 and the 
right subplot of Fig. 5, where the more accurate calibrated wind speeds lead to more precise power predictions.

Additional experiments of wind power forecasting
In this section, to further demonstrate the effectiveness of C-LSTM, we have conducted additional experiments, 
which include an exploration of weekly and monthly correlations, as well as the application of our wind speed 
calibration method to other effective wind speed forecasting models. Specifically, C-LSTM initially utilized only 
the actual wind speed from the previous day for calibration. Considering the potential periodicity in wind speed, 
we also attempted to use wind speed data from one week and one month prior for calibration. However, the 
results presented in Table 3 indicate that the wind speed data from one week or one month ago did not help 
the calibration of the forecasted wind speed, and the wind power forecasting performance remained similar to 
that before calibration. We hypothesize that this is primarily because the wind speed data from one week or one 
month ago is too temporally distant to provide meaningful improvements in wind speed calibration and wind 
power forecasting.
To demonstrate the generalizability of our adaptive wind speed calibration method, we also applied the 
method to other efficient wind power forecasting models, including Bi-LSTM42, CNN-LSTM43, Transformer44,

Conclusion
This study introduces C-LSTM, a pioneering model that integrates an adaptive calibration mechanism within 
the traditional LSTM architecture to calibrate forecasted wind speeds. By dynamically fusing historical and 
forecasted wind speeds through trainable parameters, C-LSTM significantly enhances wind power forecasting 
accuracy. Experiments conducted across 25 diverse wind turbines confirm C-LSTM’s outstanding performance, 
boosting accuracy by 0.4% and reducing MSE, N_RMSE and N_MAE by 0.012, 0.013 and 0.010 compared to 
uncalibrated forecasts. Compared to the use of historical wind speed data alone, it further increases accuracy 
by 0.5% and cuts MSE, N_RMSE and N_MAE by 0.019, 0.016 and 0.012. These improvements highlight the 
effectiveness of C-LSTM’s adaptive approach in refining wind speed predictions. The model’s success in wind 
power forecasting not only underscores its potential for enhancing grid management and operational efficiency 
in wind farms but also suggests broader applicability. C-LSTM’s approach to calibrating weather forecasts holds 
potential for transferability to other applications, such as photovoltaic power and electricity demand forecasting, 
thereby contributing to more comprehensive and reliable renewable energy integration strategies.
